The increasing width of the confidence intervals across the different horizons directly reflects the fundamental principle that forecasting inherently becomes more uncertain the further out in time we look. Despite the comprehensive nature of these intervals, certain specific risks or "tail events" could push outcomes far outside the stated ranges. These might include severe, unforeseen economic shocks such as a sudden recession, an unexpected financial crisis, or a major global supply chain collapse, which could trigger a sharp downward spiral. Conversely, a breakthrough technological innovation or an unexpected major market catalyst could send values significantly higher. Furthermore, unforeseen policy changes, like sudden interest rate hikes or new regulatory frameworks, or widespread natural disasters and health crises, possess the potential to dramatically alter economic conditions and market sentiment beyond our current probabilistic expectations.
